intro.t: The biggest of the prophets, and the most quoted.
b: Judgment on Judah and the nations, then some of the clearest promises in the Old Testament of a coming king and a suffering Servant. Chapters 40–55 address the exile directly and contain the four Servant Songs, of which Isaiah 53 is the fourth.
The New Testament quotes Isaiah more than any book except Psalms.

1.t: An ox knows its owner; Israel does not know. Isaiah opens by calling heaven and earth as witnesses.

1.h: I have had enough of burnt offerings
1.t: God rejects worship offered by people who ignore the orphan and the widow. Then: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.

6.t: Isaiah sees the LORD on a throne and is undone. John says Isaiah saw Christ's glory and spoke of him.
His first reaction to seeing God is not comfort but ruin, and specifically about his lips — the tool of his trade.
A message that will harden rather than convert. Quoted by Jesus, Paul and John.

7.t: The sign given to Ahaz. Matthew reads it as fulfilled in the virgin birth; the Hebrew word can mean young woman, and the Greek translators used the word for virgin two centuries before Christ.

9.t: Galilee of the nations named centuries before Jesus' ministry there. Matthew quotes it.

9.h: Unto us a child is born
9.t: Four titles, one of which is Mighty God — a phrase used again two chapters later, at 10:21, of the LORD himself.

40.t: The turn of the book. The voice in the wilderness is applied to John the Baptist by all four Gospels.
A sustained argument for God's incomparability, ending with the stars called out by name. It is the ground for the promise in verse 31.

40.h: They will run and not grow weary
40.t: The chapter that begins with comfort ends with strength, and the argument between them is about who God is.

42.t: The Servant will not break a bruised reed. The Father's words at Jesus' baptism draw on verse 1.

42.h: A bruised reed he will not break
42.t: The Servant's gentleness stated before his power. Matthew applies it to Jesus' habit of avoiding confrontation.

45.h: I am the LORD, and there is no other
45.t: Including the difficult line about creating light and darkness, prosperity and disaster. Isaiah refuses a tidy dualism.
God swears by himself that to him every knee will bow. Paul applies these words to Jesus in Philippians 2 and to God in Romans 14.

53.t: Pierced for our transgressions, the punishment that brought us peace, the LORD laying on him the iniquity of us all. The clearest Old Testament statement of substitution, and the passage the Ethiopian was reading in Acts 8.
Each of us turned to our own way, and the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all. Substitution stated in a single verse.
The hardest line in the chapter, and the one that makes the cross purposeful rather than tragic. He will see his offspring and be satisfied.

55.t: Buy without money. Grace stated seven centuries before the cross.
And the word that goes out and does not return empty. The passage is about God's purposes outrunning our understanding of them.

61.h: The year of the Lord's favour
61.t: The passage Jesus read at Nazareth, stopping mid-sentence before the day of vengeance.

11.t: The line of David cut down to a stump, and a shoot coming from it. The Spirit rests on him, and the peace described reaches the whole creation.

25.t: A banquet for all peoples, the shroud over the nations removed, and every tear wiped away. Revelation 21 quotes it.

30.t: In repentance and rest is your salvation — and then the honest note: but you would have none of it.

35.t: A highway called the Way of Holiness. Jesus alludes to verses 5 and 6 when John's disciples ask if he is the one.

43.h: I have called you by name
43.t: Passing through waters and fire. The promise is presence, not exemption.
You are my witnesses, so that you may know and believe that I am he. John puts the same phrase on Jesus' lips in chapter 13.

49.t: The Servant's task is too small if it is only to restore Israel. Paul and Barnabas quote it in Acts 13.
Can a mother forget her child? Even she may — I will not.

58.t: Not bowed heads but loosing chains, sharing bread, housing the homeless. One of the sharpest passages in the prophets on worship divorced from justice.

64.t: All our righteous acts. The verse is often quoted about sin; it is actually about our best efforts.

66.h: This is the one I esteem
66.t: Humble and contrite in spirit, and trembling at my word. The book ends where it began, with what God actually looks for.

14.t: Addressed to the king of Babylon, and read by many since as also describing the fall of Satan. The primary reference in the text is the king.

26.t: You will keep in perfect peace the one whose mind is steadfast. The Hebrew literally doubles the word for peace.

41.h: Do not fear, for I am with you
41.t: I will strengthen you, help you, uphold you with my righteous right hand. Three verbs, all in the first person.

44.h: The man who makes an idol
44.t: He burns half the log to cook his dinner and worships the other half. The mockery is deliberate and devastating.
God says he stretched out the heavens by himself and spread out the earth alone, and then asks who was with him. The question is rhetorical and it excludes help.

48.t: I have refined you, though not as silver. Testing described as purposeful rather than punitive.

52.t: Of those who bring good news. Paul quotes it in Romans 10 as the basis of preaching.
Chapter 53 actually starts here, with the Servant raised and lifted up — the same words used of the LORD in chapter 6.

57.t: Who lives with the contrite and lowly in spirit. Both halves of the sentence matter.

59.t: The arm of the LORD is not short; sin has separated. The diagnosis before the remedy.

65.h: New heavens and a new earth
65.t: Isaiah's vision that Revelation 21 draws on directly.

2.t: All nations stream to God's mountain and learn war no more. The same vision appears in Micah 4.

3.t: God takes away every support of the city. Verse 12: youths oppress my people, women rule over them — a picture of collapse, not a rule about leadership.

4.t: A canopy of glory over Zion, like the cloud in the wilderness. Restoration after cleansing.

5.t: God planted it carefully and it produced wild grapes. He looked for justice and saw bloodshed — a pun in the Hebrew.

8.h: Do not fear what they fear
8.t: Peter quotes this in his first letter. The LORD is the one to regard as holy.

10.h: Assyria, the rod of my anger
10.t: God uses Assyria, and then judges it for its pride. He uses nations without approving them.

12.h: In that day you will say
12.t: A short hymn of praise closing the first section. With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation.

13.t: The first oracle against the nations. Babylon here is both a real empire and a symbol, as in Revelation.

15.h: My heart cries out for Moab
15.t: The prophet grieves over the enemy he pronounces judgement on.

16.t: In the middle of an oracle against Moab, a promise of a just king from David's line.

17.h: You have forgotten God your Saviour
17.t: Damascus and Israel judged together for forgetting the Rock.

18.t: Even distant Cush will bring tribute to Zion. The nations are drawn in.

19.t: An astonishing promise: Egypt and Assyria worshipping alongside Israel, all three blessed. Old Testament universalism of the most striking kind.

20.t: Isaiah walks naked as a sign against trusting Egypt. The prophets performed what they preached.

21.t: Morning is coming, and also the night. An enigmatic oracle often read devotionally.

22.t: For tomorrow we die. Paul quotes it in 1 Corinthians 15 as the logic of a life without resurrection.

23.t: The great trading city brought low. Revelation 18's lament over Babylon draws on this chapter.

24.t: The 'Isaiah apocalypse' begins: judgement on a global scale, with God reigning on Mount Zion at the end.

27.t: The sea monster slain by God's sword. Ancient imagery of chaos used to describe God's final victory over evil.

28.t: A precious cornerstone in Zion; whoever trusts will not be dismayed. Quoted by Paul and Peter of Christ.

29.h: Their hearts are far from me
29.t: Jesus quotes it against the Pharisees in Mark 7.

31.h: Woe to those who go down to Egypt
31.t: Trusting horses and chariots rather than the Holy One of Israel.

32.h: A king will reign in righteousness
32.t: Each man like a shelter from the wind. The noble man makes noble plans.

33.h: The LORD is our judge, lawgiver, king
33.t: Three functions of government united in God.

34.t: A dark oracle using the imagery of total devastation. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

36.t: Assyria's envoy mocks trust in God in the hearing of the people on the wall. Nearly identical to 2 Kings 18.

37.t: He spreads the letter before the LORD. The answer comes through Isaiah, and 185,000 Assyrians die in the night.

38.t: Written after his recovery. For it was for my welfare that I had great bitterness.

39.t: Hezekiah displays his wealth to Babylonian envoys. Isaiah predicts Babylon will carry it all away.

46.t: The idols of Babylon are loaded onto animals; God carries his people from birth to old age.

47.t: The proud city sits in the dust. Its boast — I am, and there is none besides me — is God's own title.

50.t: He gives his back to those who strike him and his cheeks to those who pull out his beard. The Gospels' passion accounts echo it.

51.t: Consider Abraham, who was one when I called him. God's past faithfulness as the ground of present hope.

54.t: Paul quotes it in Galatians 4. My unfailing love for you will not be shaken, though the mountains depart.

56.t: Those excluded under the old law are welcomed with a name better than sons and daughters. The eunuch of Acts 8 was reading nearby.

60.t: The nations come to your light. Revelation 21 draws on the whole chapter for the new Jerusalem.

62.t: No longer called Deserted, but My Delight Is in Her. God rejoicing over his people as a bridegroom over his bride.

63.t: The warrior treading the winepress alone. Revelation 19 uses the image of the returning Christ.
